newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police face full fury of protesters.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police face full fury of protesters.

text.p: The small huddle of riot police stood no chance against the fury of the crowd.
Pushed back against a glass facade of a bar in this Adriatic port, the police withstood for a time a hail of stones against their plastic shields.
From a terrace above, a gang of youth then rained rocks, tables and chairs down on their blue crash helmets.
Within seconds, the bar was a shattered wreck and the battered group of around 30 policemen had no alternative but to surrender.
The throng of youths trampled police shields underfoot and forced them to strip off their uniforms, which were tossed onto a huge bonfire. Black smoke billowed through the desolate city centre.
Frenzy and hysteria were everywhere on the sixth day of anti-government rallies, begun as spontaneous marches last week following the collapse of a local pyramid investment fund.
Three men died in two days of clashes, one of bullet wounds and two of heart attacks, according to hospital staff.
Residents were convinced they were tackling not regular police but special forces dispatched by President Sali Berisha to retake control of the city from peaceful demonstrators.
Berisha has become the focus of hatred for tens of thousands of protesters who say the government has stolen their money lost in the shady investment schemes.
Anyone unlucky enough to be accused of working for the secret police was singled out for severe beatings.
"They take our money and now they spend it on mercenaries to come and beat us," said Xhemil, a ragged protester in his late teens.
Stones ricocheted against a thin line of police, first one at a time, then hundreds at once.
Elderly men and women smashed up paving stones by the side of the road to keep younger demonstrators constantly supplied with ammunition.

Police fought back, but their lines quickly fell apart and many beat a hasty retreat to hills overlooking the city. From that vantage point, their shields glinted in the warm winter sun as they watched protesters regain control of the city.
Protesters were rushed from the city centre, blood streaming from their faces. Many police suffered the additional indignity of being evacuated in their underwear.
"Police can only work here at night," shouted Shabani, a jubiliant young man. "During the day it's ours. Berisha is finished."
Rumours flowed through the crowd that dozens of men had been arrested late on Sunday. Without any official confirmation, the enraged crowd moved on the police station.

Battle was swiftly joined. Police perched on adjacent rooftops hurled lumps of concrete down on protesters below, though without appearing to hit their target. Demonstrators sent back a fresh hail of stones.
A lone water cannon made a doomed sortie to disperse the masses. It soon ran out of water and retreated, its reinforced windscreen smashed by well-aimed rocks.
Gunfire rattled from the direction of the police station and cars, coloured flags flying from open windows, sped out of the area to carry the wounded to hospital.
"Do you see, we're living under a fascist government that has turned on its own people," screamed a woman in her 60s.

With police pinned down inside the building and the stream of projectiles slowed, parents brought small children out on to rubble-strewn streets to survey the damage and jeer at police still waiting on the surrounding hills.
"They might come down again but we're ready for them," said protester Nikolla. "We don't want war, we just want our money back. If they push us, we'll fight to the end. We have nothing left to lose."
